dhpak2.2:1.1: 2.2 The Story about the Rich Man Kumbhaghosaka
dhpak2.2:2.1: “For he who is active, mindful,” {1.231} this Dhamma teaching was given by
dhpak2.2:2.2: the Teacher while he was in residence at Veḷuvana with reference to Kumbhaghosaka.
dhpak2.2:3.1: For once upon a time the snake-wind disease broke out at Rājagaha in the house of the
dhpak2.2:3.2: principal rich man of Rājagaha. When the snake-wind disease breaks out, animals, from flies to cattle, are the
dhpak2.2:3.3: first to die; after them, slaves and workers; after them, the master and mistress of a household.
dhpak2.2:4.1: So this disease attacked last of all the rich man and his wife. As soon as they felt the first
dhpak2.2:4.2: touch of the disease, they looked at their son, who stood near, and with eyes filled with tears said to
dhpak2.2:4.3: him: “Dear son, as we know, when this disease breaks out, only those who break down the wall and flee
dhpak2.2:4.4: succeed in saving their lives. Therefore have no consideration for us, but make your escape. Having thus saved your life,
dhpak2.2:4.5: come back again, and in such and such a place you will find buried in the [28.294] earth 400
dhpak2.2:4.6: million of treasure. Dig up the treasure and live on the money.” {1.232} When the son heard his parents speak
dhpak2.2:4.7: thus, he wept aloud, paid homage to his mother and father, and terrified with the fear of death, broke down
dhpak2.2:4.8: the wall and fled. Seeking refuge in a certain mountain jungle, he dwelt there for twelve years, and then returned.
dhpak2.2:5.1: Now since he was a mere boy when he went away, and when he returned his hair and beard had
dhpak2.2:5.2: grown long, no one recognized him. A sign which his mother and father had given him enabled him to find
dhpak2.2:5.3: the place where the treasure had been buried, and going there he discovered that the treasure had not been disturbed.
dhpak2.2:5.4: But he thought to himself: “No one knows me here, and if I dig up this treasure and begin
dhpak2.2:5.5: to spend it, they will say: ‘A treasure has been dug up by a certain poor man,’ and will seize
dhpak2.2:5.6: me and subject me to annoyance. Suppose I were to work for hire and thus gain a living?” So he
dhpak2.2:5.7: dressed himself in rags and went through the servants’ quarters, inquiring: “Is there anyone who has need of a servant?”
dhpak2.2:6.1: When the servants saw him, they said: “If you will do a certain piece of work for us, we will pay
dhpak2.2:6.2: you for it with food.” – “What kind of work is it, friends?’” – “To order and direct our work. You
dhpak2.2:6.3: will be obliged to get up early in the morning and go the rounds of the workers and give orders to
dhpak2.2:6.4: them, saying: ‘Men, get up and bring out the carts and yoke the oxen; it is time for the elephants and
dhpak2.2:6.5: horses to go to pasture. Women, you also get up and cook broth and rice.’” – “Very well,” said the rich
dhpak2.2:6.6: man, accepting the task. So they gave him a house to live in, and he did his work faithfully every day.
dhpak2.2:7.1: Now one day King Bimbisāra, who understood all sounds, heard his voice and straightaway said: “That is the voice of
dhpak2.2:7.2: some rich man.” A certain female servant who stood near {1.233} thought to herself: “No matter what the king says,
dhpak2.2:7.3: this is something I ought to investigate.” Therefore she sent out a man, saying to him: “Just go and find
dhpak2.2:7.4: out who this is.” The messenger straightaway went and looked at the man, and on his return made the following report:
dhpak2.2:7.5: “That is a poor man who is a hired worker among hired workers.” When the king heard his report, he
dhpak2.2:7.6: said nothing; but on the second day and on the third day, hearing his voice, said precisely the same thing.
dhpak2.2:8.1: Every time the king made this remark the same thought occurred to that female servant, and again and again she
dhpak2.2:8.2: sent a man to investigate. Every time she heard the report: “That is a poor man,” she [28.295] thought to
dhpak2.2:8.3: herself: “Every time the king hears the report: ‘That is a poor man,’ he refuses to believe it, and keeps
dhpak2.2:8.4: repeating: ‘That is the voice of some rich man.’ There must be a reason for this, and it is
dhpak2.2:8.5: my duty to find out the real facts.” Accordingly she said to the king: “Your majesty, give me a thousand
dhpak2.2:8.6: coins, and I will take my daughter and go to this man and bring his treasure to the royal palace.”
dhpak2.2:9.1: The king caused a thousand coins to be given to her. She took the money, caused her daughter to put on
dhpak2.2:9.2: a soiled dress, and departed with her from the royal palace. Pretending that she was making a journey, she went to
dhpak2.2:9.3: the servants’ quarters, and entering a certain house, said to the mistress: “Woman, we are making a journey and should like
dhpak2.2:9.4: to rest here for a day or two before we go on.” – “Woman, there are many persons living in this
dhpak2.2:9.5: house, and it is out of the question for you to remain here. But Kumbhaghosaka’s house is empty; go there.”
dhpak2.2:9.6: So she went there and said to Kumbhaghosaka: “Master, we are making a journey and should like to remain here a
dhpak2.2:9.7: day or two.” He refused her request, although she repeated it again and again. Finally she said: “Master, we will remain
dhpak2.2:9.8: here today, just for one day, and early in the morning will continue our journey.” So saying, she refused to depart.
dhpak2.2:10.1: So she took up her residence there. On the following day, when it was time for Kumbhaghosaka to go
dhpak2.2:10.2: to the forest, she said to him: “Master, give me an allowance for food {1.234} before you go,
dhpak2.2:10.3: and I will cook food for you.” – “Never mind about that,” replied Kumbhaghosaka, “I will cook food all
dhpak2.2:10.4: by myself and eat it.” After she had urged him repeatedly, he gave her the allowance. As soon as
dhpak2.2:10.5: she received it, she procured from a shop cooking-vessels and the purest of rice. Preparing the finest of boiled
dhpak2.2:10.6: rice in the manner of cooking practiced in the king’s household, and cooking with the greatest care two
dhpak2.2:10.7: or three portions of sauce and curry, she presented the food to Kumbhaghosaka on his return from the forest.
dhpak2.2:11.1: When he had eaten his meal and his heart had softened, she said to him: “Master, we are tired and
dhpak2.2:11.2: will remain here for a day or two.” – “Very well,” he said, consenting to the arrangement. Likewise in the
dhpak2.2:11.3: evening and on the following day she cooked savory food for him and gave it to him. When she
dhpak2.2:11.4: perceived that his heart had softened, she said to him: “Master, we will remain right here for a few days.”
dhpak2.2:12.1: Thus she contrived to establish a residence in his house. One day she took a sharp knife and cut the webbing
dhpak2.2:12.2: of his bed underneath at [28.296] the bed-frame in several places. The result was that, when he returned and sat on
dhpak2.2:12.3: his bed, the webbing sank down. He said: “How did this bed come to be cut in this fashion?” – “Master,
dhpak2.2:12.4: I cannot prevent the boys from coming here and jumping on it.” – “Woman, it is because of you that
dhpak2.2:12.5: I have been subjected to this annoyance. Before you came, whenever I wished to go anywhere, I closed the door and
dhpak2.2:12.6: went.” – “My friend, what shall I do? I cannot stop them.” For two or three days she cut the webbing
dhpak2.2:12.7: of his bed in this way, and when he became irritated and angry and rebuked her, she made the same answer.
dhpak2.2:13.1: Finally she cut all of the cords except one or two. {1.235} On that day, as soon as he sat on
dhpak2.2:13.2: the bed, the entire webbing fell to the ground, and he was doubled up with his head between his knees.
dhpak2.2:13.3: Rising to his feet, he said: “What shall I do? Where shall I go now? I have no longer a bed
dhpak2.2:13.4: on which I can lie.” – “Dear friend, what can I do? I cannot prevent the boys of the neighborhood
dhpak2.2:13.5: from entering. Well, do not worry. Let me think where you might go at this time.” And addressing her daughter, she
dhpak2.2:13.6: said to her: “My dear daughter, make room for your brother to lie down.” So her daughter lay down on
dhpak2.2:13.7: one side of her bed and said to Kumbhaghosaka: “Master, come lie here.” The mother also said to him: “Dear friend,
dhpak2.2:13.8: go lie with your sister.” Accordingly Kumbhaghosaka lay down on the same bed with the girl and that very night
dhpak2.2:13.9: he had intercourse with her. The young girl burst into tears. Her mother asked her: “Dear daughter, why are you weeping?”
dhpak2.2:13.10: – “Mother, such and such happened.” – “Well, what’s to be done about it? You ought to have a husband,
dhpak2.2:13.11: and he ought to have a wife.” So she made Kumbhaghosaka her son-in-law, and thereafter Kumbhaghosaka and her daughter lived together.
dhpak2.2:14.1: After a few days she sent a message to the king, saying: “Cause the following proclamation to be made:
dhpak2.2:14.2: ‘Let those who dwell in the servants’ quarters make holiday. Whoever does not make holiday in his house shall
dhpak2.2:14.3: be visited with such and such punishment.’” The king did so. Kumbhaghosaka’s mother-in-law said to Kumbhaghosaka: “Dear son the
dhpak2.2:14.4: king commands those who dwell in the servants’ quarters to make holiday. What shall we do?” – “Mother, I
dhpak2.2:14.5: can barely get along on the wages I earn. What shall I do?” – “Dear son, those who live
dhpak2.2:14.6: in a house of their own can borrow money. {1.236} The king’s command must not be disobeyed, but a
dhpak2.2:14.7: debt can be paid off in some way or other. Go somewhere and get one or two coins.” [28.297]
dhpak2.2:15.1: Kumbhaghosaka, much provoked, went to the spot where his 400 million of treasure were buried, removed but
dhpak2.2:15.2: a single piece of money, and returned with it. His mother-in-law sent this piece of money to
dhpak2.2:15.3: the king and paid the expenses of the holiday with a piece of money of her own.
dhpak2.2:16.1: Again after a few days she sent the same message to the king. Again the king gave orders: “Let
dhpak2.2:16.2: them make holiday. Those who do not shall be visited with such and such punishment.” And again Kumbhaghosaka, under
dhpak2.2:16.3: compulsion of his mother-in-law, who repeated the same suggestion she had previously made, went to his hidden store,
dhpak2.2:16.4: removed three coins, and brought and gave them to her. She sent these three pieces also to the king.
dhpak2.2:17.1: After a few days more had passed, she sent yet another message to the king, saying: “Now let the
dhpak2.2:17.2: king send some of his men and summon this man into his presence.” The king’s men came and began a
dhpak2.2:17.3: search for their man, inquiring: “Which man is Kumbhaghosaka?” When they saw Kumbhaghosaka, they said to him: “Come, sir,
dhpak2.2:17.4: the king summons you.” Kumbhaghosaka was frightened and was unwilling to go, saying: “The king does not know me,” and
dhpak2.2:17.5: much else. But the king’s men overpowered him, and seizing him by the hands and feet, dragged him off.
dhpak2.2:18.1: When his mother-in-law saw what they were doing, she reviled them, saying: “Rascally villains, you are not fit to lay
dhpak2.2:18.2: hands on my son-in-law.” Turning to Kumbhaghosaka, she said: “Go, my dear son; be not afraid. When I see the
dhpak2.2:18.3: king, I will have him cut off the hands of those who seized you by the hands and feet.” So
dhpak2.2:18.4: saying, she took her daughter, and preceding the king’s men, went to the royal palace. When she arrived at the
dhpak2.2:18.5: palace, she changed her garments, adorned herself with all her adornments, and thus arrayed took her stand on one side.
dhpak2.2:19.1: The king’s men came, pulling and dragging Kumbhaghosaka with them. Kumbhaghosaka worshipped the king and took his stand before
dhpak2.2:19.2: him. The king said to him: “You are Kumbhaghosaka?” – “Yes, your majesty.” – “Why do you conceal your great
dhpak2.2:19.3: wealth and live as you do?” {1.237} – “Where is my great wealth, your majesty? I make a living
dhpak2.2:19.4: by working for hire.” – “Do not act thus. Why do you deceive us?” – “I am not deceiving you,
dhpak2.2:19.5: your majesty. I have no wealth.” Then the king showed him those coins and asked him: “Whose are these
dhpak2.2:19.6: coins?” Kumbhaghosaka recognized the coins. He thought: “What a fool I am! How did these coins get into the
dhpak2.2:19.7: hands of the king?” Looking about him, he saw [28.298] those two women, adorned and bejeweled, standing at the door
dhpak2.2:19.8: of the room. He thought: “This is a deep-laid plot. These women must have been suborned by the king.”
dhpak2.2:20.1: Then the king said to him: “Speak, sir. Why do you act thus?” – “I have no protector, your majesty.”
dhpak2.2:20.2: – “There does not exist a protector who is my equal.” – “Your majesty, it would be most agreeable to
dhpak2.2:20.3: me if your majesty were my protector.” – “That am I, sir. How great is your wealth?” – “400 million, your
dhpak2.2:20.4: majesty.” – “What shall I send to convey your wealth here?” – “Carts, your majesty.” So the king had several
dhpak2.2:20.5: hundred carts yoked, and sent and had Kumbhaghosaka’s wealth brought and heaped up in the palace court. Then he assembled
dhpak2.2:20.6: the residents of Rājagaha and asked: “Is there anyone at all in this city that possesses so much wealth as this?”
dhpak2.2:20.7: – “There is not, your majesty.” – “What should be bestowed upon him?” – “Honor, your majesty.” So the king
dhpak2.2:20.8: bestowed high honor upon him, appointed him to the post of Rich Man, and gave him his daughter in marriage.
dhpak2.2:21.1: The king then took Kumbhaghosaka to the Teacher, worshipped the Teacher, and said to him: “Venerable Sir, behold this
dhpak2.2:21.2: man. For steadfastness the like of his does not exist. Though he possesses 400 million of treasure, he
dhpak2.2:21.3: gives no sign of being unduly elated, nor is he puffed up in his own conceit. As though he
dhpak2.2:21.4: were a poor man, {1.238} he dressed himself in rags and worked for his living in the servants’ quarter.
dhpak2.2:21.5: In this way I came to know of him. And coming to know of him, I sent for him,
dhpak2.2:21.6: made him admit his wealth, caused his wealth to be carried to the palace, appointed him to the
dhpak2.2:21.7: post of rich man, and gave him my daughter in marriage. So steadfast a man I never saw before.”
dhpak2.2:22.1: Hearing this, the Teacher said: “If a man lives thus, great king, his life is a righteous life. But
dhpak2.2:22.2: the deeds of thieves and other wicked men oppress and harm them in this world and in the next;
dhpak2.2:22.3: no happiness comes from them. For if a man, when his wealth is exhausted, farms or works for
dhpak2.2:22.4: hire, his life is a righteous life. For such a man, exerting the power of his manhood, always mindful,
dhpak2.2:22.5: pure in deeds and words, circumspect of conduct through wisdom, exercising self-restraint in deeds and words and thoughts, leading
dhpak2.2:22.6: a righteous life, never relaxing mindfulness, such a man grows in prosperity.” So saying, he pronounced the following verse:
dhpak2.2:23.1: For he who is active, mindful, pure in deeds and
dhpak2.2:23.2: considerate, self-controlled, living by Dhamma, heedful, fame greatly increases.
dhpak2.2:25.1: At the conclusion of the verse Kumbhaghosaka was established in Stream-entry, and many others reached the
dhpak2.2:25.2: fruition of Stream-entry and so on. Thus, benefit arose to many people from the Dhamma teaching.
